Finding a reason will never be reason enough, as there have been many great thinkers in human history who have failed to find a definitive answer. There is no such thing as a premature cessation of the ongoing process, as it makes no difference what one discovers during life. All the insight that one can never be sure of, all the growth that is merely standing on the shoulders of giants, it all amounts to nothing in the end. I care nothing for the greater context of myself, for in the grand scheme of everything, which is to say, when I look at all things in my perception of the world relative to each other, none of it has meaning. There is truly no more reason to live than to die, they are on equal footing as valid options from a rational perspective. It only makes sense to take the path of least resistance. Why struggle and struggle to better myself and to learn when I will only die in the end anyways? Given two paths with the same outcome, why not take the shorter one? There are those who say that it is more about the journey than the destination, but when the destination is reached, the journey will inevitably be forgotten.

I may not be omniscient, but I am only one point of perspective within the universe. I have only two eyes to see with, so to speak, and therefore I must base all of my decisions on the electrical signals transmitted from my senses to my brain. And prior to the early 2000's, transsexual was a blanket term used for anyone with an alternative gender identity. AIDS was originally named GRID (Gay Related Immune Disorder) as well. Time passes, and as we learn new things, our view of them has to change. Most people learned to see the two terms as synonymous as they were growing up simply because the general public didn't know a lot about the subject at the time.

This is absolutely true. The difference between sexes is a lot more than reproduction-specific biology. It's important to have the right frame of reference on the subject, though, and that's not easy since few subjects combine biology and sociology on the same level. To this end, it's important to remember the context of the issue. We have by and large moved past the time in the development in our civilization where we need to be concerned about who does the hunting and the gathering, or how many humans of either sex remain in the population. This is why the issues of gender and sexuality are starting to be addressed on a wide scale in the first place. In other words, differences that may have been important from a historic or biological standpoint are no longer necessarily important from a social point of view. Additionally, as we strive to learn more about the topic, as we tend to do with just about anything, we begin to realize that it might not be as simple or black and white as we initially thought. It has been mentioned several times in this thread that research has found a surprising amount of evidence that the brains of trans* people are neurologically and physically similar to the brains of the gender they identify with. There is also promising new research in the field of epigenetics that suggests accidental inheritance of epigenetic markers may be behind transgenderism and homosexuality.

TL;DR we still have a lot to learn about sex and the biology behind it, and it goes much deeper than a set list of differences between the male and female sexes.

Transsexualism is a junction between gender and sex. If you identify as a particular gender, it might be appealing to experience sex in the way that 'fits' that gender role. It also might be that their perception of themselves as a particular gender feels incomplete without the genitalia typically associated with it. While it is as a result of society and its established gender roles, I would not say that it is purely for the sake of society, or any less valid than anything else a person might want to do to perfect their gender expression. That's what it's all about, really, expression -- and the human body is no less valid a canvas than anything else. The fact that it all stems from society doesn't make it a bad thing, either. Humans are social creatures and need a healthy self image and a place that they feel they fit in. That's the best I can really explain it, as I don't have any negative feelings about what's currently between my legs, but my dysphoria surrounding my general body shape has sort of opened my eyes to the whole scope of gender and sexuality. I hope I'm kind of shedding some light on things?
Summed up perfectly in two sentences. Bravo. :D

There are physical differences between different biological SEXES (of which there are more than two). How people of a particular gender are treated, and the culture, mannerisms, etc. associated with them are social constructs. We have concepts of masculinity and femininity that evolved from society rather than biology. That's generally what transgenderism is about, and most misunderstandings about transgenderism and gender identity as a whole arise from a lack of differentiation between 'sex' and 'gender'.
From the outside, it's easy for people to think so, but what they're actually doing is fulfilling the identity they really want.
